subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the points of intersection of the perpendicular tangents to an ellipse lie on a circle.

mark_split.label: Set up the tangent through P

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.63 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 72. NOT on an SSP page. Printed appearance: AP 16 only. Book p.63 prints no margin mark tags for this proof-style question, so the 1+1+1+1 split here is OURS, following the four natural stages of the standard 'product of roots' proof. This same result (director circle x²+y²=a²+b²) is repeated verbatim in the Bullet Model Paper's SAQ Section B (book p.107, under 'Q11: CIRCLES' as a worked model, not under Ellipse) — that repeat is a different chapter's worked example reusing this proof and is not treated as an extra card. A FIGURE is authored for this card — the ellipse, its director circle, and one external point with two perpendicular tangent lines touching the ellipse — because the picture IS the argument here: seeing that the locus point sits on a circle concentric with the ellipse is the entire content of the result being proved. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: The name 'director circle' for x² + y² = a² + b² is worth writing on the final boxed line — examiners often award the last mark for naming the result, not just deriving it.

steps.label: Set up the tangent through P
steps.margin_note: First mark. A tangent with slope m always has the form y = mx ± √(a²m² + b²).
steps.memory_tip: Start every 'tangents through a point' proof the same way: write the tangent-with-slope-m formula, then force it through the given point.
lines: Let the ellipse be S ≡ x²/a² + y²/b² − 1 = 0
Let P(x₁, y₁) be a point on the locus.
Tangent with slope m: y = mx ± √(a²m² + b²)
If it passes through P(x₁, y₁):
steps.why: Forcing the general tangent line to pass through the locus point P turns the geometric condition ('a tangent through P') into an algebraic equation relating m to the coordinates of P.
common_mistakes: Substituting P into the ellipse equation itself instead of into the tangent line equation.
Dropping the ± sign, which represents the fact that two tangents (not one) generally pass through an external point.

steps.label: Form the quadratic in m
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Squaring removes the root and produces a quadratic whose two roots are the two tangent slopes.
steps.memory_tip: Two tangents from one point means: look for a QUADRATIC whose two roots are their two slopes.
steps.why: Equation (1) is a quadratic in m; its two roots m₁, m₂ are exactly the slopes of the two tangents that pass through P, since each root satisfies the tangency condition.
common_mistakes: Expanding (y₁ − mx₁)² incorrectly and losing the cross term −2mx₁y₁.
Forgetting that this is now an equation in m (unknown), with x₁, y₁ as fixed constants.

steps.label: Apply the perpendicularity condition
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Perpendicular tangents mean the product of the two roots m₁m₂ = −1.
steps.memory_tip: Product of roots of am² + bm + c = 0 is c/a — apply it here with a = (x₁²−a²), c = (y₁²−b²).
lines: If the tangents are perpendicular, m₁m₂ = −1
steps.why: Two lines are perpendicular exactly when the product of their slopes is −1; since m₁ and m₂ are the roots of the quadratic in (1), their product is read off directly from the ratio of its constant and leading coefficients.
common_mistakes: Using sum of roots instead of product of roots — perpendicularity is a PRODUCT condition, not a sum.
Missing the minus sign when writing the ratio of the constant term to the leading coefficient.

steps.label: Conclude the locus
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Clear the fraction and simplify — the x₁² and a² terms combine into a circle equation.
steps.memory_tip: The director circle is centred at the same centre as the ellipse, with radius √(a² + b²).
lines: y₁² − b² = −(x₁² − a²) ⇒ x₁² + y₁² = a² + b²

lines.text: x² + y² = a² + b² — director circle

steps.why: Rearranging the perpendicularity equation shows that every point from which the two tangents are perpendicular satisfies x² + y² = a² + b², which is the equation of a circle concentric with the ellipse.
common_mistakes: Stopping at y₁² − b² = a² − x₁² without moving all terms to one side to reveal the circle equation.
Forgetting to name the result — the locus is called the director circle.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: No marks — the question does not ask for a diagram. Drawn because the picture IS the argument here.
steps.memory_tip: The director circle is always bigger than the ellipse and shares its centre.
steps.why: P sits on the director circle, and the two tangent lines from P touch the ellipse at right angles to each other — the whole content of the theorem is visible in this one picture.
common_mistakes: Drawing the two tangent lines from P as if they were parallel rather than perpendicular.
Drawing the circle smaller than or equal to the ellipse — the director circle is always strictly larger.
